stories.headline: Can Nifty, Sensex rally further or will bears reign in? 5 factors to steer market this week
stories.title: Can Nifty, Sensex rally further or will bears reign in? 5 factors to steer market this week
stories.summary: Benchmark indices Sensex and Nifty extended gains for a second consecutive session on Friday. Continued strength in IT stocks, which rose for a fourth straight session, along with buying in auto, metal and PSU banking stocks, supported the rally.Looking ahead, the 22,800–22,750 zone remains a crucial support. As long as Nifty sustains above 22,750, the recovery is likely to extend. On the upside, 23,400–23,450 remains the immediate resistance zone, a decisive breakout above which could propel the index towards 23,650, coinciding with its 100-day EMA.Here are 5 factors that investors need to watch out for1.) Q2 earnings - Banking heavyweights HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and Axis Bank all declared their earnings on Saturday. Investors will assess loan growth, deposit mobilisation, margins, asset quality and management commentary for cues on earnings momentum, credit demand and the outlook for the financial sector.India’s largest private lender HDFC Bank on Saturday reported a net profit of Rs 19,510 crore for the second quarter of FY27, marking a 4.6% jump from Rs 18,641 crore posted in the same period last year. HDFC Bank’s net interest income (interest earned less interest expended) for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, grew 9.7% to Rs 34,620 crore from Rs 31,550 crore in the corresponding quarter last year.2.) Oil prices - Crude oil prices climbed sharply higher on Friday to clinch $110 for the first time since May as Iran intensified attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi militants launched missiles at Saudi Arabia and Ukraine pledged to resume strikes on Russian refineries, fuelling concerns over global energy supplies.Markets remain uncertain about how the conflict will develop. JPMorgan analysts said the war’s eventual trajectory was difficult to model. At the outset, the bank had expected the US administration to avoid crossing certain economic thresholds. Seven months into the conflict, many of those thresholds had been crossed, while a clear exit strategy remained elusive.3.) IT stocks - IT stocks such as TCS, Tech Mahindra, Infosys and Wipro had a strong week, rallying up to 17% and lifting the index by 12% over the week amid better-than-expected earnings and a sharp plunge in AI-linked stocks.Additionally, Nifty IT is firmly placed in the leading quadrant of the RRG, indicating strong relative strength and momentum. On the daily chart, the index is on the cusp of breaking its lower-low, lower-high structure. The 32,000–32,200 zone is the immediate resistance. A decisive and sustained move above this zone could pave the way for a continuation of the pullback in the near term, Sudeep Shah of SBI Securities said.4.) FII activity - Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) remained net sellers for the ninth consecutive week, but outflows eased sharply to Rs 8,991 crore from Rs 30,294 crore in the previous week, according to Bajaj broking.FIIs turned net buyers of Rs 1,166 crore on Friday. Domestic institutional investors (DIIs), meanwhile, remained net buyers for the ninth straight week, with inflows of Rs 7,813 crore, despite net selling of Rs 3,661 crore on Friday. Month-to-date, DII net buying of Rs 48,168 crore has almost entirely offset FII net selling of Rs 48,769 crore.Going ahead, the moderation in FII outflows suggests that market sentiment may be stabilising, although elevated crude oil prices continue to pose a risk to the recovery. Investors will track Brent crude prices and developments in US-Iran relations, while domestic attention will remain on Q2FY27 earnings, Pabitro Mukherjee of Bajaj Broking said.5.) Rupee up for 5th session - The Indian rupee rose 2% this week to record its strongest weekly gain in seven months, supported by policy measures aimed at stabilising the currency. However, analysts cautioned that a sustained recovery would depend on easing the underlying pressures on the rupee.The currency closed at Rs 94.96 per US dollar, up 0.1% on the day, recovering after last week’s slide brought it close to its record low of Rs 96.96 per dollar.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Veer Sharma, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. stories.headline: Starlink: The Promise and the Risk
stories.title: Starlink: The Promise and the Risk
stories.summary: India should welcome new technology, foreign investment and competition in telecommunications. But it must also recognise that some commercial services can become matters of national security. When communications networks are used by the armed forces, emergency services and critical public institutions, their availability cannot be left entirely to commercial considerations. The controversy surrounding Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service has brought this question into focus. Musk’s public clash with Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani is ostensibly about competition, market access and consumer choice. But the larger issue is whether India can afford to become excessively dependent on a critical communications network controlled by a foreign private company. Ukraine’s experience offers an important lesson. According to Reuters, Ukrainian military operations faced disruption in October after restrictions were imposed on satellite communications supporting drone missions. A Reuters report on October 15 said the reported order to limit access to the military-oriented Starshield system had come from within the White House. The service was subsequently restored following discussions between the US and British defence leadership. An important distinction must be made here. Starlink provides satellite broadband services, while Starshield is a separate, military-oriented system developed by SpaceX for government and defence applications. Nevertheless, the episode raises a serious question: what happens when a country becomes dependent on a communications network whose operations are controlled by a private company based abroad? The fact remains, Ukraine has benefited enormously from Starlink since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. The service helped keep hospitals, government offices and emergency services connected when conventional communications infrastructure was damaged. It also became important for military communications and drone operations. Starlink has played an important role in helping Ukraine withstand the crisis. But its recent experience also shows that over-reliance on a privately run network can pose a security risk when circumstances change. India needs to learn from this. It does not mean that Starlink is unsafe or that American technology should be avoided. The point is simple: no country should depend so heavily on a foreign-controlled communication network that its national security is at risk if that service is disrupted or restricted. India must have reliable alternatives of its own. Elon Musk has accused influential Indian business interests of trying to obstruct Starlink’s entry to protect their existing market positions. In a sarcastic remark, as national media reported, directed at Ambani, he used the expression “Prime Minister Ambani”, arguing that competition would give consumers more choices and encourage companies to offer better services at affordable prices. Reliance, in its October 16 statement, said it had never feared competition and welcomed satellite communications services, including Starlink. It also said its own satellite services were awaiting government clearances and maintained that Indian and foreign operators should be governed by the same rules. Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has said that three operators — Starlink, Reliance Jio’s satellite venture and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, have received licences, subject to the remaining requirements for commercial operations. There are important, legitimate questions about the pace of regulatory clearances and whether established companies are trying to protect their market positions. These issues should be examined on the basis of facts and transparent rules, rather than through public exchanges between wealthy businessmen. But the debate must not end there. Even if every allegation of commercial lobbying were proved wrong, New Delhi’s security concerns would and should remain. Similarly, even if Starlink offered the most attractive prices, affordability alone would not settle the question of strategic dependence. Satellite internet can bring benefits to a country as geographically diverse as India. It can connect remote Himalayan villages, islands, border settlements, ships and disaster-hit areas where laying fibre-optic cables is difficult or uneconomical. We agree that people living in remote regions need better connectivity to improve access to education, healthcare, banking and government services. Businesses can also benefit from more reliable communication. Starlink’s established technology and extensive satellite constellation could help expand connectivity in underserved areas. India should not deny these advantages merely because the service is foreign-owned. However, satellite networks differ from conventional telecom infrastructure. A terrestrial internet provider relies substantially on infrastructure located within the country. Satellite broadband depends on spacecraft in orbit, ground equipment, specialised terminals, software and a network operated by a company headquartered abroad. Indian authorities can regulate services offered within the country, but independently verifying every aspect of a complex satellite network presents a different challenge. The first concern is continuity of service. What would happen if a foreign operator restricted connectivity during a military confrontation, border emergency or diplomatic dispute? Would hospitals, emergency services and security agencies be able to continue their work? The second concern is data security. Satellite networks can generate information about users, terminals, locations and network activity. Some of this information may be commercially valuable, while other data could have security implications. India must establish enforceable safeguards governing the collection, storage, processing and sharing of such information. The most important issue is operational control and compliance with Indian law. It cannot be taken in a lighter way. Authorities, in all circumstances, should be able to address unlawful use, enforce legitimate restrictions and ensure that satellite services meet the country’s regulatory requirements. These safeguards become particularly important in sensitive border areas and strategically significant locations. These are genuine policy questions, not arguments for protectionism. The country should also not be dependent on a single point of dependence India’s digital transformation has made communications infrastructure essential to banking, commerce, public services, defence and disaster management. A disruption that once affected a limited number of users can now have consequences for entire systems. Consider a major earthquake, flood or other disaster that damages terrestrial networks. Satellite internet could become invaluable when conventional communication lines fail. But if the satellite service itself becomes unavailable, or its capacity is restricted at the very moment it is needed most, the country could face another crisis. The answer is not to reject satellite technology but to ensure that no single network becomes the only option. The same principle applies to national security. India cannot assume that a commercial service will remain available under every geopolitical circumstance. Equally, it should not presume that a foreign company will necessarily act against Indian interests. National planning must be based on safeguards and alternatives, rather than either assumption. This concern is not just about Elon Musk or the United States. The same questions would arise if a company from any other country controlled a communication network on which India depended for its critical needs. Allowing a foreign company to provide a service is one thing; depending on it for essential national functions is quite another. The first gives people more choices and improves connectivity. The second calls for much greater caution. India, now one of the leading global powers, should neither shut its doors to Starlink nor let a dispute between two business leaders decide the country’s technology policy. The government must encourage new technology and investment while ensuring that national interests are not compromised. First, there should be clear rules for all satellite service providers on data protection, security, access to information by lawful authorities and accountability. Indian and foreign companies should follow the same standards. Second, the government must ensure that essential communication services continue to work during emergencies. Defence establishments, disaster management agencies and other critical services should have access to alternative networks. These arrangements must also be tested regularly so that the country is not caught unprepared if one service is disrupted or restricted. Third, India needs to strengthen its own satellite technology and infrastructure. Indian companies and research institutions should get the support needed to develop local expertise and capabilities. Depending too much on a single foreign provider can limit the country’s options during a crisis. A mix of domestic and foreign services would give India greater flexibility. Finally, all decisions on satellite services must be foolproof and based on complete national security, technical needs and the public interest. They should not be influenced by pressure from technological giants, powerful business groups, or political considerations. Competition is important, but companies must also be held accountable for their services. Ukraine’s experience shows that technology can be a great help during a crisis, but it can also create new problems. A communication network that works well in normal times may become a source of concern when political relations change, or a conflict intensifies. The lesson for New Delhi is clear. India should neither shield domestic companies from competition nor reject foreign technology without reason. It must, however, ensure that dependence on any one company does not put the country at risk at a crucial moment: man-made or natural disaster. India should welcome new technology, guard completely against its risks and protect its strategic independence. Author is National Editor, Greater Kashmir

stories.headline: Rubio cites India’s energy needs, US ties to defend Russia sanctions waiver
stories.title: Rubio cites India’s energy needs, US ties to defend Russia sanctions waiver
stories.summary: Marco Rubio defended a 60-day waiver on Russia-linked sanctions, citing India’s importance to Washington and its continued reliance on Russian energy
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

opening: Marco Rubio defended a 60-day waiver on Russia-linked sanctions, citing India’s importance to Washington and its continued reliance on Russian energy.
The US government has opted to lift specific sanctions concerning the import of Russian oil and gas.
body: This includes a review period of 60 days to evaluate the economic effects on key importers such as India and China.
Senator Marco Rubio highlighted India's persistent dependency on Russian energy sources despite attempts to explore alternatives.
US President Donald Trump is taking 60 days to assess the global and domestic economic impact of sanctions on Russia and tariffs on countries buying Russian oil.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the waivers offer relief to India amid energy uncertainties.

US President Donald Trump wants to take a 60-day period to analyse what imposing sanctions on Russia and tariffs on other countries would mean for the global economy, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said here.
Rubio was responding to questions on Saturday evening ahead of his departure for a week-long tour of Uzbekistan and India.

"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy, and even to the US economy," Rubio said in response to a question on the waivers granted by Trump under the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act or the Graham Act.
On Friday, Trump waived key provisions of the Graham Act that authorised punitive tariffs on countries purchasing Russian oil, offering relief to India.
The executive order signed by Trump on Friday states that the waivers shall remain in effect until such time as the President or the Secretary of State, in consultation with the Secretary of the.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Directs States, UTs To Notify Anti-Human Trafficking Units As Police Station
stories.title: Supreme Court Directs States, UTs To Notify Anti-Human Trafficking Units As Police Station
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court has directed all States and Union Territories to take steps to confer police station status on Anti-Human Trafficking Units (ATHUs) by issuing appropriate notifications in accordance with law, emphasising that the measure is necessary for the effective implementation of its Victim Protection Plan to combat human trafficking.
A bench of Justice J.B. Pardiwala and Justice R. Mahadevan directed the Home Departments of all States and Union Territories to give effect to the direction at the earliest.
It also asked the Union Government to take up the issue with all States and UTs and ensure that the necessary notifications are issued.

The direction came during an ongoing hearing in which the Court reviewed compliance with its May 29, 2026 judgment concerning human trafficking of women and children for commercial sexual exploitation.

Senior Advocate Aparna Bhat, appearing for the petitioner, brought to the Court's attention that ATHUs needed to be given the status of police stations in accordance with paragraph 362(b)(iii) of the main judgment.

“In this regard, we direct all the State/UT Governments in their respective Home Departments to give effect to this direction at the earliest by issuing an appropriate notification, in accordance with law.”
The Court added that the Union Government “shall also take up this issue at the earliest with all the States/UTs and see to it that appropriate notifications are issued.”
The direction forms part of the Court's broader effort to ensure effective implementation of the Victim Protection Plan framed under Article 142 of the Constitution.
The bench noted that the four additional directions issued in paragraph 456 of its main judgment had not been fully complied with by all States and UTs.

These include notifying recognised welfare institutions under Sections 15(6A) and 17A of the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956; preparing State- and UT-wide lists of eligible social welfare workers; and designating.

Officers.

stories.headline: Supreme Court grants bail to former Rajasthan Minister in Jal Jeevan Mission case
stories.title: Supreme Court grants bail to former Rajasthan Minister in Jal Jeevan Mission case
stories.summary: The Justices ordered the release of Mukesh Pathak, another accused, setting aside an August 13 order of the Rajasthan High Court denying regular bail
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

article_sentences: The Supreme Court of India granted bail on Friday (October 16, 2026) to former Congress Minister Mahesh Joshi in connection with the alleged Jal Jeevan Mission scam, observing that prolonged pre-trial detention cannot be allowed to “degenerate into punishment without trial” in breach of constitutional guarantees.

A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu also ordered the release of Mukesh Pathak, another accused in the case, setting aside an August 13 order of the Rajasthan High Court denying them regular bail.

“There can be no gainsaying that allegations of large-scale financial impropriety and institutional collusion in the execution of a public welfare project such as the ‘Jal Jeevan Mission’ are grave and warrant serious scrutiny.
We think the State is justified in opposing the grant of bail to persons accused of involvement in such extensive criminal activity.

Nevertheless, the gravity of the allegations, however serious, cannot by itself eclipse all other considerations governing the grant of bail or justify indefinite pre-trial detention,” the Bench said.
The court noted that the investigation against both accused was complete and chargesheets had been filed.
The prosecution's case rests overwhelmingly on documentary and electronic evidence already in the investigating agency’s custody.
It added that the possibility of tampering with such evidence had been “substantially obviated” and that neither accused was required for further custodial interrogation or recovery.
The case stems from an Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) probe into alleged irregularities in tenders floated by Rajasthan’s Public Health Engineering Department (PHED) under the Jal Jeevan Mission.

According to the prosecution, two firms participated in 237 tenders between 2021 and 2023 using forged work completion certificates and letters of acceptance purportedly issued by IRCON International Limited.
The firms allegedly emerged as the lowest bidders on the strength of these credentials and secured work orders in 104 tenders worth a combined ₹979.45 crore.
The Bench noted that the case involves 22 accused, three chargesheets, 124 prosecution witnesses, and 20,000 pages of documents.
